doc.title: Orrin Keepnews interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Francisco, California, August 7, 2002

chapter: Later careers of Cannonball, Monk and Evans
title: Cannonball's later career versus Wes Montgomery and Monk at Columbia
summary: Cannonball kept control of his work, unlike Wes and Monk at their later labels.

blocks.x: Right. Well it’s funny, it’s almost the same thing with rock bands. They have a hit and people want to hear it, but those things are fortunate for the bands I think. Did you feel good about what happened with Cannonball’s music and career in later years when he was with Capitol and so forth?

Well it’s funny, the answer always has to be yes and no. Because I’ll always — if I look at somebody who went on and it happened to practically everybody. I mean for instance if you ask me that question about Wes Montgomery I would have no trouble saying definitely not did I think that what happened to Wes was terrible and very possibly shortened his life because I know that he was pretty uptight about being put into this pop bag and playing all these heavily arranged and pop-derived material but Cannon pretty much retained control over what he was doing. To the extent that when — I mean I mentioned that he and I were back together at Fantasy and that was at a point where yeah I was the VP running the jazz program at Fantasy but Cannon was in there on a contract that gave him pretty much control over what he did. And he started out, he and I both enjoyed the fact that I was taking care of my business, he was taking care of his. I wasn’t involved in his record dates. Then we ran into some problems mainly with a couple of his albums being seriously over budget and such and the situation was getting a little strained between artist and label and I was asked to step in and see if I could heal the breach and so I ended up actually on I think the last two albums that Cannonball did at Fantasy before he died. There actually are three producers on each of those albums. They’re produced by Cannon, Nat and me. And actually we did work together on it. But in a sense we had been working together back in the old days too. So I would say that what happened to his career, it’s always been tragic the way it was cut short. The man had a stroke and never regained consciousness. And he was only in his 40s. But I didn’t feel badly about that, I felt I wasn’t happy with what happened to Monk’s career at Columbia where for the most part, there were a few exceptions and there were a couple of interesting big band things, but for the most part it was the working group over and over again, and Monk and I had been very happy with the variations that we were able to do and the interesting guests and associations that we were able to bring in, I just think that what happened there was he took the path of least resistance, nobody really gave him — because there were some large things where like “Big Band at Lincoln Center,” a live performance big band stuff. The final Monk record for Columbia which was the Oliver Nelson arrangements I thought just lost the whole spirit of Monk so badly that it was not a good record.
